subject: Current Affairs
q: The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is designed to:
o: Pay developing countries to protect forests
Put a carbon price on certain imports into the EU
Ban petrol cars at EU borders
explanation: CBAM charges importers of carbon-intensive goods such as steel and cement for embedded emissions to prevent "carbon leakage".

subject: Current Affairs
q: "Net zero" emissions means:
o: A country produces no industrial goods
Emissions released are balanced by an equivalent amount removed from the atmosphere
Emissions are cut by half compared with 1990
explanation: Net zero is reached when any remaining greenhouse gas emissions are offset by removals, for example through forests or carbon capture.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Ramsar Convention of 1971 is concerned with the conservation of:
explanation: The Convention on Wetlands, signed at Ramsar in Iran, protects wetlands of international importance.

subject: Current Affairs
q: CITES regulates:
o: International trade in endangered species of wild animals and plants
explanation: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species ensures that trade in wild specimens does not threaten their survival.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Basel Convention controls the transboundary movement of:
explanation: The 1989 Basel Convention aims to stop the dumping of hazardous waste from developed to developing countries.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Stockholm Convention of 2001 targets:
explanation: The Stockholm Convention seeks to eliminate or restrict chemicals such as DDT and PCBs that persist in the environment.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Minamata Convention is an international treaty to protect human health from:
explanation: Named after the Japanese city poisoned by mercury pollution, the 2013 Convention controls mercury mining, use and emissions.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework of 2022 set a target to protect by 2030:
o: 30 per cent of the world's land and oceans
explanation: Adopted under the Convention on Biological Diversity, the "30 by 30" target is its best-known goal.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 provides that Antarctica shall be used:
o: As a shared zone for oil exploration
As a nuclear testing ground under UN control
For the fishing rights of Southern Hemisphere states
Only for peaceful purposes and scientific research
explanation: The Treaty bans military activity and nuclear explosions in Antarctica and freezes territorial claims.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 prohibits:
o: Placing nuclear weapons in orbit or on celestial bodies
explanation: It declares space the province of all humankind, bars national appropriation of celestial bodies and bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) was opened for signature in:
explanation: The NPT was opened for signature in July 1968 and entered into force in 1970.

subject: Current Affairs
q: At the 1995 Review and Extension Conference, the NPT was:
explanation: Parties decided in 1995 to extend the treaty indefinitely, 25 years after it entered into force.

subject: Current Affairs
q: Under the NPT, a "nuclear-weapon state" is one that had manufactured and exploded a nuclear device before:
explanation: This cut-off date recognises only the USA, Russia, UK, France and China as nuclear-weapon states under the treaty.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The three pillars of the NPT are non-proliferation, disarmament and:
o: The peaceful use of nuclear energy
explanation: The treaty balances non-proliferation obligations with a commitment to disarmament and the right to peaceful nuclear energy.

subject: Current Affairs
q: NPT Review Conferences are held every:
explanation: Article VIII provides for review conferences, which have been held at five-year intervals since 1975.

subject: Current Affairs
q: Which country announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003?
explanation: North Korea announced its withdrawal in January 2003 and conducted its first nuclear test in 2006.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) was adopted by the UN General Assembly in:
explanation: The CTBT, banning all nuclear explosions, was adopted in September 1996 but has not yet entered into force.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The CTBT has not entered into force because:
o: The UN Security Council has not approved it
Several of the 44 states listed in its Annex 2 have not ratified it
The IAEA has declined to verify it
explanation: Entry into force requires ratification by all 44 Annex 2 states holding nuclear technology, and several, including the USA, China, India and North Korea, have not ratified.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Preparatory Commission for the CTBT Organization, which runs the global test-monitoring system, is based in:
explanation: The CTBTO Preparatory Commission operates the International Monitoring System from Vienna.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear tests:
o: In the atmosphere, outer space and under water
explanation: The PTBT, signed by the USA, USSR and UK, banned tests except underground.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The proposed Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty (FMCT) would ban:
o: The production of fissile material for nuclear weapons
The transfer of nuclear weapons between allies
explanation: The FMCT would stop the production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for weapons; negotiations have long been stalled at the Conference on Disarmament.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Conference on Disarmament, the world's single multilateral disarmament negotiating forum, meets in:
explanation: The CD, which negotiated the Chemical Weapons Convention and the CTBT, meets in Geneva and works by consensus.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which entered into force in 2021, was adopted in:
explanation: The TPNW was adopted in July 2017; none of the nuclear-armed states has joined it.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) of 2015 concerned:
o: Nuclear cooperation between India and the USA
A nuclear-free zone in the Middle East
Limits on Iran's nuclear programme in return for sanctions relief
explanation: Iran agreed with the P5+1 and the EU to restrict its nuclear programme under IAEA verification in exchange for the lifting of sanctions.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The United States withdrew from the Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) in:
explanation: President Trump announced the US withdrawal in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions on Iran.

subject: Current Affairs
q: In the Iran nuclear negotiations, "P5+1" refers to the five permanent members of the Security Council plus:
explanation: The P5+1 group was the USA, UK, France, Russia, China and Germany, often joined by the EU.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty of 1987, from which the USA withdrew in 2019, was signed between the USA and:
explanation: Reagan and Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty, which eliminated ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500–5,500 km.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Treaty of Tlatelolco established a nuclear-weapon-free zone in:
explanation: Signed in 1967, Tlatelolco created the first nuclear-weapon-free zone in a densely populated region.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Treaty of Pelindaba created a nuclear-weapon-free zone covering:
explanation: The Pelindaba Treaty was signed in 1996 and entered into force in 2009; Semipalatinsk covers Central Asia and Rarotonga the South Pacific.

subject: Current Affairs
q: In 2008 the Nuclear Suppliers Group granted a special waiver allowing civil nuclear trade with India, following India's nuclear agreement with:
explanation: The India–US Civil Nuclear Agreement (the "123 Agreement") led to the NSG waiver of September 2008 despite India being outside the NPT.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR) seeks to limit the spread of:
o: Missiles and unmanned systems capable of delivering weapons of mass destruction
explanation: Created by G7 countries in 1987, the MTCR is an informal arrangement coordinating export controls on missile technology.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Biological Weapons Convention, the first treaty to ban an entire category of weapons of mass destruction, was opened for signature in:
explanation: The BWC was opened for signature in 1972 and entered into force in 1975; the Chemical Weapons Convention followed in 1993.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Chemical Weapons Convention, implemented by the OPCW, was signed in:
explanation: The CWC was opened for signature in 1993 and entered into force in 1997, banning the development, production and use of chemical weapons.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Ottawa Treaty of 1997 bans:
explanation: The Mine Ban Convention prohibits the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel mines.

subject: Current Affairs
q: A "nuclear triad" refers to the ability to deliver nuclear weapons from:
o: Land-based missiles, submarines and strategic bombers
explanation: A triad gives a state survivable delivery options across land, sea and air.

subject: Current Affairs
q: "Second-strike capability" means a state's ability to:
o: Strike an adversary twice in one day
Retaliate with nuclear weapons after absorbing a first nuclear attack
explanation: A secure second-strike capability, often based on submarines, underpins deterrence by guaranteeing retaliation.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Cold War doctrine of "MAD" held that nuclear war would be deterred because:
o: Each side could destroy the other even after being attacked
Nuclear weapons had been banned by treaty
Only one side possessed nuclear weapons
explanation: Mutually Assured Destruction rested on the certainty that any nuclear attack would provoke devastating retaliation.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The "Most-Favoured-Nation" principle of the WTO requires a member to:
o: Extend any trade advantage given to one member to all other members
Treat foreign goods better than domestic goods
Impose equal tariffs on all products
explanation: MFN is the principle of non-discrimination between trading partners, set out in Article I of GATT.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The WTO principle of "national treatment" means that:
o: Every country may set its own tariffs without limits
National governments control all foreign trade
Nationals of a country receive visas automatically
Imported goods, once they have entered the market, must be treated no less favourably than local goods
explanation: National treatment prohibits discrimination between imported and domestically produced goods after customs clearance.

subject: Current Affairs
q: In the WTO system, TRIPS refers to the agreement on:
o: Trade Rules for Investment and Public Services
Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights
explanation: The TRIPS Agreement sets minimum standards for patents, copyright and trademarks among WTO members.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The WTO agreement covering trade in services is called:
explanation: The General Agreement on Trade in Services extended multilateral trade rules to services such as banking and telecommunications.

subject: Current Affairs
q: In international trade, "dumping" means:
o: Banning imports from a rival country
Exporting goods at a price lower than their normal value in the home market
Dumping industrial waste in the sea
Devaluing a currency to boost exports
explanation: WTO rules permit anti-dumping duties when dumped imports cause material injury to a domestic industry.

subject: Current Affairs
q: What distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
o: Members allow free movement of labour
Members adopt a common external tariff towards non-members
explanation: Both remove internal tariffs, but only a customs union also sets a common tariff on imports from outside countries.

subject: Current Affairs
q: A common market goes beyond a customs union by allowing:
o: Free movement of labour and capital among members
explanation: A common market adds the free movement of factors of production to the free trade and common tariff of a customs union.

subject: Current Affairs
q: A policy of restricting imports through tariffs and quotas to shield domestic industries is known as:
explanation: Protectionism aims to protect local producers from foreign competition, in contrast to free-trade policies.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The "Washington Consensus" refers to a set of policy prescriptions emphasising:
o: Fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation and privatisation
Debt cancellation for all developing countries
explanation: The term, coined in 1989, described the market-oriented reforms promoted by the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury for developing countries.

subject: Current Affairs
q: Which country withdrew from negotiations on the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2019?
explanation: India pulled out, citing concerns over trade deficits, particularly with China; the other 15 countries signed RCEP in 2020.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, often described as the world's largest free trade agreement, entered into force in:
explanation: Signed in November 2020, RCEP took effect on 1 January 2022 for its first ratifying members.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The United States withdrew from the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) in:
explanation: President Trump withdrew in January 2017; the remaining eleven countries went ahead with the CPTPP in 2018.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The trade war between the United States and China, marked by rounds of tariffs on each other's goods, began in:
explanation: The USA imposed tariffs on Chinese imports in 2018, and China retaliated, disrupting global supply chains.

subject: Current Affairs
q: "De-dollarisation" refers to efforts by some countries to:
o: Reduce their reliance on the US dollar in trade and reserves
Replace their currencies with the US dollar
explanation: Countries such as Russia and China have sought to settle trade in local currencies and diversify reserves away from the dollar.

subject: Current Affairs
q: In 2022 several Russian banks were cut off from SWIFT, which is:
o: A global messaging network for international bank payments
explanation: SWIFT, based in Belgium, carries payment instructions between banks worldwide, so exclusion hampers cross-border transactions.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The "price cap" introduced by the G7 and EU in December 2022 applied to seaborne exports of:
explanation: The cap barred Western firms from providing shipping and insurance services for Russian oil sold above a set price, to reduce Russia's revenues.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Human Development Index published by the UNDP combines indicators of health, education and:
explanation: The HDI measures life expectancy, schooling and gross national income per capita.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The term "Global South" generally refers to:
o: Countries in the Southern Hemisphere only
Developing and emerging countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America
Countries that border the South Pole
explanation: The term is political and economic rather than strictly geographical; it includes countries such as India and Pakistan north of the equator.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Paris Club is an informal group of:
o: Central banks that set interest rates
Official creditor countries that coordinate debt relief
explanation: Since 1956 the Paris Club has helped debtor countries restructure bilateral official debt.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The global financial crisis of 2008 was triggered mainly by the collapse of:
o: Oil prices after the Gulf War
explanation: Defaults on risky US housing loans spread through financial markets, causing bank failures such as Lehman Brothers and a worldwide recession.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Asian financial crisis of 1997 began in:
explanation: It started with the collapse of the Thai baht in July 1997 and spread across East and South-East Asia.

subject: Current Affairs
q: In 2022, which South Asian country defaulted on its external debt for the first time in its history?
explanation: Sri Lanka suspended foreign debt payments in April 2022 amid a severe foreign-exchange and economic crisis.

subject: Current Affairs
q: In 2017 Sri Lanka leased the Hambantota port to a Chinese company for:
explanation: Unable to service loans for the port, Sri Lanka leased it to China Merchants Port Holdings for 99 years, fuelling debates on debt and strategic influence.

subject: Current Affairs
q: An economic condition combining high inflation with stagnant growth and high unemployment is called:
explanation: Stagflation, seen after the 1970s oil shocks, is hard to address because measures against inflation can deepen unemployment.

subject: Current Affairs
q: China's Belt and Road Initiative was announced by President Xi Jinping in:
explanation: Xi announced the Silk Road Economic Belt in Kazakhstan and the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road in Indonesia in 2013.

subject: Current Affairs
q: President Xi Jinping first announced the Silk Road Economic Belt in 2013 during a speech in:
explanation: The land component of the BRI was unveiled at Nazarbayev University in Astana in September 2013; the maritime component was announced in Indonesia a month later.

subject: Current Affairs
q: IMEC, announced on the sidelines of the G20 summit in New Delhi in 2023, stands for:
explanation: IMEC envisages shipping and rail links from India through the Gulf and Israel to Europe, backed by the USA, EU, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

subject: Current Affairs
q: Global Gateway, launched in 2021 as an infrastructure investment strategy for developing countries, belongs to:
explanation: The EU's Global Gateway aims to mobilise investment in connectivity, energy and digital projects, widely seen as an alternative to China's BRI.

subject: Current Affairs
q: India has invested in developing the Chabahar port located in:
explanation: Chabahar, on Iran's Makran coast near Gwadar, gives India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia bypassing Pakistan.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC) is a multimodal route connecting India with Russia through:
explanation: The INSTC, agreed by India, Iran and Russia in 2000, combines sea, rail and road routes via Iran and the Caspian region.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The "Middle Corridor" (Trans-Caspian International Transport Route) links China and Europe via:
o: Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey
explanation: Interest in the Middle Corridor grew after 2022 as a route that bypasses Russia.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Northern Sea Route, which is becoming more navigable as Arctic ice melts, runs along the coast of:
explanation: The route along Russia's Arctic coast shortens voyages between East Asia and Europe compared with the Suez route.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The term "String of Pearls" describes:
o: China's network of ports and facilities across the Indian Ocean
India's chain of islands in the Bay of Bengal
A series of US naval bases in the Pacific
explanation: The phrase, coined by US analysts, refers to Chinese-linked ports from the South China Sea to East Africa, seen as extending Chinese strategic reach.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Strait of Malacca separates:
explanation: The Strait of Malacca links the Indian Ocean with the South China Sea and is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The "Malacca Dilemma" refers to the vulnerability of which country's energy imports passing through the Strait of Malacca?
explanation: Most of China's oil imports pass through the strait, which could be blockaded in a conflict; CPEC and Myanmar pipelines are seen as partial alternatives.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and:
explanation: The strait separates Iran from the Musandam peninsula of Oman and carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil.

subject: Current Affairs
q: From late 2023, attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden were carried out by:
explanation: The Houthis targeted ships they linked to Israel and its supporters during the Gaza war, forcing many carriers to reroute around Africa.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean Sea with the:
explanation: Opened in 1869, the canal allows ships to travel between Europe and Asia without going around Africa.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Suez Crisis of 1956 began when the canal was nationalised by:
explanation: Nasser's nationalisation led Britain, France and Israel to invade Egypt; US and Soviet pressure forced their withdrawal.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The United States handed full control of the Panama Canal to Panama in:
explanation: Under the 1977 Torrijos–Carter Treaties, control of the canal, linking the Atlantic and Pacific, passed to Panama on 31 December 1999.

subject: Current Affairs
q: Passage of warships through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles is governed by the:
explanation: The Montreux Convention gives Turkey control over the straits and limits the passage of warships of non-Black Sea states.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Strait of Gibraltar connects the Atlantic Ocean with the:
explanation: The strait separates Spain in Europe from Morocco in Africa.

subject: Current Affairs
q: The Palk Strait separates India from:
explanation: The narrow Palk Strait lies between Tamil Nadu and northern Sri Lanka.
